summary.text: Take the composite number \(n=23492890653051=3\cdot37\cdot43\cdot42307\cdot116341\). The gcd-sum equals the multiplicative function \(\sum_{d\mid n}\varphi(d)(n/d)\), whose value at a prime \(p\) is \(2p-1\); hence it is \(5\cdot73\cdot85\cdot84613\cdot232681=610815156979325=26n-1\), so the denominator gcd is \(n\) and the resulting value is \(1\).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
G(n)=\sum_{k=1}^{n}\gcd(k,n),
\qquad
 a(n)=\frac{n}{\gcd(n,1+G(n))}.
\]
We will exhibit a composite positive integer \(n\) for which \(a(n)=1\).

We first derive the form of the gcd-sum that will make the calculation manageable. Recall the standard totient identity
\[
m=\sum_{d\mid m}\varphi(d)
\]
for every positive integer \(m\), where \(\varphi\) is Euler's totient function. Applying this with \(m=\gcd(k,n)\) gives
\[
\gcd(k,n)=\sum_{d\mid \gcd(k,n)}\varphi(d).
\]
A positive integer \(d\) divides \(\gcd(k,n)\) exactly when it divides both \(k\) and \(n\). Therefore
\[
\begin{aligned}
G(n)
 &=\sum_{k=1}^{n}\sum_{d\mid\gcd(k,n)}\varphi(d)\\
 &=\sum_{k=1}^{n}\sum_{\substack{d\mid n\\d\mid k}}\varphi(d).
\end{aligned}
\]
Interchanging these two finite sums yields
\[
G(n)=\sum_{d\mid n}\varphi(d)\,\#\{k:1\leq k\leq n,\ d\mid k\}.
\]
If \(d\mid n\), the multiples of \(d\) in the interval from \(1\) through \(n\) are
\(d,2d,\ldots,(n/d)d\), so there are exactly \(n/d\) of them. Consequently,
\[
\boxed{G(n)=\sum_{d\mid n}\varphi(d)\frac nd.}\tag{1}
\]

It is also useful to note that the right-hand side of (1) is multiplicative. More precisely, if \(r\) and \(s\) are coprime, then every divisor of \(rs\) has a unique expression \(uv\), where \(u\mid r\) and \(v\mid s\). Moreover, \(u\) and \(v\) are coprime, so
\(\varphi(uv)=\varphi(u)\varphi(v)\), and
\[
\frac{rs}{uv}=\frac ru\frac sv.
\]
Thus (1) gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
G(rs)
 &=\sum_{u\mid r}\sum_{v\mid s}
   \varphi(uv)\frac{rs}{uv}\\
 &=\sum_{u\mid r}\sum_{v\mid s}
   \left(\varphi(u)\frac ru\right)
   \left(\varphi(v)\frac sv\right)\\
 &=G(r)G(s).
\end{aligned}\tag{2}
\]
Hence \(G\) is multiplicative on coprime arguments.

For a prime \(p\), the only divisors are \(1\) and \(p\). Since \(\varphi(1)=1\) and \(\varphi(p)=p-1\), formula (1) gives
\[
G(p)=\varphi(1)p+\varphi(p)\cdot1=p+(p-1)=2p-1.\tag{3}
\]

Now take
\[
n=23492890653051.
\]
It has the factorization
\[
\begin{aligned}
n
 &=3\cdot37\cdot43\cdot42307\cdot116341.
\end{aligned}\tag{4}
\]
For clarity, the successive products in (4) are
\[
3,\quad111,\quad4773,\quad201931311,\quad23492890653051,
\]
which checks the displayed factorization.

The five factors in (4) are distinct primes. For the small factors this is immediate for \(3\), and trial division by primes no larger than their square roots proves primality of \(37\) and \(43\): neither is divisible by \(2,3,5\), and \(\sqrt{37},\sqrt{43}<7\). For the two larger factors, the same finite primality criterion applies. Since
\[
205^2=42025<42307<42436=206^2,
\]
division by every prime at most \(205\) gives a nonzero remainder for \(42307\). Likewise,
\[
341^2=116281<116341<116964=342^2,
\]
and division by every prime at most \(341\) gives a nonzero remainder for \(116341\). Thus neither larger number has a prime divisor at most its square root, and both are prime. This finite trial-division calculation establishes precisely the primality needed here. In particular, all five factors in (4) are pairwise coprime.

We may therefore repeatedly apply multiplicativity (2), followed by the prime evaluation (3). This gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
G(n)
 &=G(3)G(37)G(43)G(42307)G(116341)\\
 &=(2\cdot3-1)(2\cdot37-1)(2\cdot43-1)
   (2\cdot42307-1)(2\cdot116341-1)\\
 &=5\cdot73\cdot85\cdot84613\cdot232681.
\end{aligned}
\]
The successive products in this last computation are
\[
5,\quad365,\quad31025,\quad2625118325,
\quad610815156979325.
\]
Hence
\[
G(n)=610815156979325.
\]
Adding one, we obtain
\[
1+G(n)=610815156979326.
\]
Direct multiplication using the value of \(n\) gives
\[
26n=26\cdot23492890653051=610815156979326,
\]
so
\[
1+G(n)=26n.\tag{5}
\]
Equation (5) says in particular that \(n\mid 1+G(n)\). Therefore
\[
\gcd(n,1+G(n))=\gcd(n,26n)=n.
\]
Since \(n>0\), it follows that
\[
a(n)=\frac{n}{\gcd(n,1+G(n))}=\frac nn=1.\tag{6}
\]

It remains to check that this value of \(n\) does not satisfy either of the two alternatives asserted by the conjecture. Certainly
\(n=23492890653051\neq1\). It is also not prime: from (4),
\[
n=3\cdot7830963551017,
\]
and both factors are greater than \(1\). Thus \(n\) is composite.

We have therefore found a positive composite integer \(n\neq1\) for which \(a(n)=1\). If the proposed equivalence held for every positive integer, applying its forward implication to (6) would force either \(n=1\) or \(n\) prime. The first case is contradicted by the displayed value of \(n\), and the second by its nontrivial factorization by \(3\). Hence the proposed characterization is false.
